title: Get Started with Bitcoin
hook: Your first steps into sound money.

sections.title: Buying Your First Bitcoin
sections.content:
The single biggest misconception that keeps people from buying Bitcoin is the belief that you need to buy a whole coin. You absolutely do not. Bitcoin is divisible down to eight decimal places — the smallest unit, called a satoshi, is worth a tiny fraction of a penny. You can buy ten dollars worth of Bitcoin right now and own roughly 10,000 satoshis. You don't need thousands of dollars to get started. You just need the willingness to take that first small step.

To buy Bitcoin, you'll use a platform that connects your bank account or debit card to the Bitcoin network. Think of it like an on-ramp from the traditional financial world to the Bitcoin world. The most beginner-friendly options in the United States include Strike, which charges zero trading fees and lets you withdraw instantly; River, which offers excellent educational content alongside a clean buying experience; and Cash App, which millions of people already have on their phones. For those in Latin America, Bitso operates across Mexico, Colombia, Brazil, and Argentina with solid reputations and local currency support. In El Salvador, Strike integrates seamlessly with the country's Bitcoin infrastructure.

The process on most platforms follows the same basic steps. Download the app, create an account (this usually requires identity verification due to financial regulations), link a bank account or debit card, and place your first purchase. The whole thing takes about fifteen minutes, most of which is waiting for identity verification to complete. Some platforms verify you instantly; others take a day or two. Once verified, buying Bitcoin is as simple as typing in a dollar amount and tapping a button.

Here's an important distinction to understand from day one: buying Bitcoin on an exchange is not the same as owning Bitcoin. When you buy on an exchange, the exchange holds your coins for you, similar to how a bank holds your deposits. This is fine as a starting point, but the whole philosophy behind Bitcoin is personal sovereignty over your money. As soon as you're comfortable, withdraw your Bitcoin to a wallet that you control. We cover this in detail in the self-custody module, but the key takeaway is simple — buy on the exchange, then move to your own wallet.

Don't try to time the market. Nobody — not professional traders, not hedge fund managers, not your friend who's 'really into crypto' — can consistently predict short-term price movements. The people who have built significant Bitcoin positions over the years didn't do it by timing perfect entries. They did it by buying consistently over time, which brings us to the most powerful strategy available to regular people: dollar-cost averaging.

sections.title: Dollar-Cost Averaging Explained
sections.content:
Dollar-cost averaging, or DCA, is the simplest and most stress-free way to accumulate Bitcoin over time. The concept is straightforward: instead of trying to buy at the perfect moment, you invest a fixed dollar amount at regular intervals — say, fifty dollars every week, or two hundred dollars on the first of every month. Sometimes you'll buy when the price is high, sometimes when it's low, but over time your average purchase price smooths out and you avoid the emotional rollercoaster of trying to time the market.

Why does DCA work so well? Because it removes emotion from the equation entirely. Bitcoin's price is volatile — it can swing ten or twenty percent in a single week. Without a DCA strategy, most people make terrible decisions driven by fear and greed. They see the price shooting up and buy impulsively at the top because they're afraid of missing out. Then they see the price crash and panic-sell at the bottom because they're afraid of losing more. Buy high, sell low — the exact opposite of what you want to do. DCA eliminates this pattern because you buy on a fixed schedule regardless of what the price is doing. Your purchases become automatic and emotionless, which historically has been the most profitable approach for the vast majority of investors.

The math backs this up compellingly. If you had invested just ten dollars per week into Bitcoin starting in January 2019, your total investment of roughly $3,600 would have been worth over $17,000 by early 2024 — nearly a five-fold return. You wouldn't have needed to check the price, follow the news, or stress about volatility. You just set it and forget it. Even people who started DCA at Bitcoin's all-time high in November 2021 — literally the worst possible timing — were back in profit within a couple of years because they kept buying through the downturn at lower prices, bringing their average cost down dramatically.

Setting up a DCA plan is simple on most platforms. Strike, River, Swan Bitcoin, and several others let you configure automatic recurring purchases — daily, weekly, biweekly, or monthly. You choose the amount and frequency, connect a funding source, and the platform handles the rest. Many also offer automatic withdrawal to your personal wallet, so your Bitcoin flows from the exchange to your own custody without you lifting a finger after the initial setup.

The best DCA strategy is the one you can stick with consistently for years. Don't overcommit. Pick an amount that won't cause you financial stress even in a tough month — an amount you genuinely won't miss. For some people that's ten dollars a week. For others it's five hundred dollars a month. The specific number matters far less than the consistency. Bitcoin rewards patience and discipline above everything else. Set your recurring buy, forget about the daily price, and let time do the heavy lifting.

sections.title: Recommended Platforms and Tools
sections.content:
Not all Bitcoin platforms are created equal, and choosing the right one can save you significant money in fees while giving you a much better experience. The platforms recommended here are selected based on three criteria that matter most: low fees, the ability to withdraw your Bitcoin to your own wallet, and a track record of reliability and trustworthiness.

For buyers in the United States, Strike stands out as the best overall starting point. It charges zero percent trading fees on Bitcoin purchases, supports instant Lightning Network payments, and lets you withdraw your Bitcoin to any wallet immediately. The interface is clean and intuitive — if you can use Venmo, you can use Strike. River is another excellent choice, particularly for people who want to set up recurring purchases and appreciate a more educational approach. River's team creates outstanding content explaining Bitcoin, and their platform is built exclusively for Bitcoin (no altcoins cluttering the interface). Swan Bitcoin caters specifically to long-term savers with automated recurring buys and an emphasis on low fees over time. Cash App is worth mentioning because so many people already have it installed — the Bitcoin buying experience is basic but functional, and withdrawals to external wallets are supported.

For buyers in Latin America, the landscape varies by country but several strong options exist. Bitso is the largest and most established exchange in the region, operating in Mexico, Colombia, Brazil, and Argentina with local currency support, reasonable fees, and reliable Bitcoin withdrawals. In El Salvador, Strike operates natively and integrates with the country's Bitcoin infrastructure, making it the obvious choice. In Argentina, where annual inflation has exceeded 100 percent in recent years, Lemon Cash has become popular for its combination of Bitcoin buying and a spending card. For Venezuelans facing limited formal exchange options, peer-to-peer trading through platforms like Bisq or Telegram communities remains a practical route to acquiring Bitcoin.

Beyond buying platforms, a few additional tools will enhance your Bitcoin experience significantly. For tracking your portfolio without connecting exchange accounts, Blockfolio (now called FTX... actually, just use CoinGecko or a simple spreadsheet). For checking real-time Bitcoin data and network statistics, mempool.space is the gold standard — it shows you pending transactions, fee estimates, and block information in a beautiful interface. For learning, follow Bitcoin-only news outlets like Bitcoin Magazine and The Bitcoin Times rather than general crypto media, which tends to mix signal with enormous amounts of noise.

A word of caution about platforms to avoid. Stay away from any platform that doesn't let you withdraw your Bitcoin to your own wallet — if you can't take your coins off the platform, you don't truly own them. Be skeptical of platforms offering unusually high 'yield' or 'interest' on your Bitcoin deposits. As the collapses of Celsius, BlockFi, and Voyager demonstrated painfully, those returns came from lending your Bitcoin to risky counterparties, and when the bets went bad, customers lost everything. If something sounds too good to be true in Bitcoin, it is. Stick with platforms that do one thing well: let you buy Bitcoin and send it to your own wallet.

sections.title: Your Bitcoin Journey Starts Now
sections.content:
You've made it through the education. You understand why money is broken, how inflation silently erodes your savings, what makes Bitcoin different from everything that came before, and how real people around the world are already using it to protect their financial futures. Now comes the part that actually matters — doing something about it.

The gap between knowing and doing is where most people get stuck forever. They read the articles, watch the videos, nod along in agreement, and then close the browser and go back to watching their purchasing power shrink by the month. Don't be that person. The difference between you and someone who actually benefits from Bitcoin isn't intelligence or technical skill — it's willingness to take that first uncomfortable step into something new.

Here is your concrete action plan, and it starts today. Step one: download a Bitcoin wallet. Blue Wallet or Muun will work perfectly. It takes two minutes. Step two: buy a small amount of Bitcoin. Even ten dollars. Use Strike, River, Cash App, or whatever platform works in your country. The amount doesn't matter — the act of doing it does. Step three: send that Bitcoin from the exchange to your own wallet. Watch it arrive. Feel what it's like to hold money that no government can print more of, no bank can freeze, and no corporation can take away. That feeling — that quiet confidence of holding something truly yours — is what brings people down the rabbit hole and keeps them there.

As Satoshi Nakamoto, Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, wrote in the original whitepaper: 'What is needed is an electronic payment system based on cryptographic proof instead of trust.' That single sentence contains the entire thesis. The current financial system runs on trust — trust that banks won't fail, trust that governments won't debase the currency, trust that the rules won't change overnight. Bitcoin runs on math. You don't have to trust anyone. You just have to verify.

Your Bitcoin journey won't end with your first purchase — it will begin there. You'll start noticing inflation differently. You'll pay attention to monetary policy for the first time. You'll have conversations with friends and family that shift their perspective too. You'll understand why millions of people around the world, from Nigerian entrepreneurs to Salvadoran business owners to Argentine savers, have already made this same choice. And ten years from now, when you look back at this moment, you'll be glad you didn't wait one more day. The best time to start was years ago. The second best time is right now.
